articles.fullText:
A sore throat, a runny nose or an earache can disrupt an ordinary day. When symptoms become uncomfortable, some people reach for antibiotics left over from a previous illness, believing they will recover faster.
But antibiotics do not work against every infection. If a sore throat is caused by a virus, for example, an antibiotic will not treat the cause. Unnecessary or incorrect use can have consequences far beyond one episode of illness.
This everyday decision is connected to a much larger threat: antimicrobial resistance (AMR). As microorganisms become resistant to medicines designed to treat them, infections can become harder to cure. Antibiotic resistance is a major part of this challenge, threatening medicines on which modern healthcare depends.
That is why World AMR Awareness Week, observed from November 18 to 24, matters to everyone. Its 2026 theme, "One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now," calls for coordinated action across human, animal and environmental health.
World Children's Day on November 20, which falls during this week, reminds us that protecting children’s health also means using antibiotics wisely so that effective medicines remain available for future generations.
A mother cares for her sick daughter and gives her medicine. 
A threat that concerns us all
A 2024 study published in The Lancet estimated that bacterial AMR was directly responsible for 1.14 million deaths worldwide in 2021. According to the study's baseline estimate, bacterial AMR could directly cause a cumulative total of 39.1 million deaths between 2025 to 2050.
These figures are a warning, not an inevitable future. AMR threatens more than the treatment of infections. Antibiotics help make major surgery, organ transplantation, cancer treatment and intensive care safer. If effective antibiotics become harder to use, many areas of modern medicine could face greater risks.
Not every sore throat needs an antibiotic
In ear, nose and throat practice, one of the most common conversations is explaining why an antibiotic may not be necessary.
Most acute sore throats are caused by viruses, against which antibiotics have no effect. Some are caused by bacteria, such as group A streptococcus, and may require treatment. A doctor's assessment and, when appropriate, testing can help identify the likely cause.
Bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics. 
Sinusitis is another common source of misunderstanding. Yellow or green nasal discharge does not automatically mean a bacterial infection; mucus color alone cannot establish the cause. The 2025 update of the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Foundation's adult sinusitis guideline advises clinicians to consider bacterial sinusitis when symptoms persist without improvement for at least 10 days, or worsen after initially getting better. For uncomplicated cases, watchful waiting may be appropriate when follow-up is assured.
Ear pain also does not automatically call for oral antibiotics. Treatment depends on the underlying condition, not the symptom alone.
When a patient asks for antibiotics, simply saying "You don't need them" is rarely enough. Doctors should explain what the examination suggests, why an antibiotic is unlikely to help, and what can relieve the symptoms. Patients also need to know when to return if their condition worsens or fails to improve.
Not prescribing an unnecessary antibiotic is not the same as doing nothing. It is a clinical decision based on likely benefit and risk. Equally, when a bacterial infection requires antibiotics, treatment should not be delayed because of concerns about resistance. The aim is not to avoid antibiotics at all costs, but to use them when they are likely to benefit the patient.
Assortment of antibiotic pills and tablets. 
Patients and doctors share responsibility
Some patients take antibiotics without medical advice, reuse leftover medicines or share prescriptions. Doctors, too, may feel pressure from limited consultation time, diagnostic uncertainty or patient expectations and prescribe "just in case." Prescribing should instead be guided by clinical evidence, appropriate testing and local resistance data.
Hospitals can support responsible use through antimicrobial management, professional education, infection surveillance and effective infection prevention. Patients should seek professional advice rather than self-medicate, and follow their clinician's instructions when antibiotics are prescribed.
Good communication is essential. When patients understand why an antibiotic is unnecessary, they are more likely to accept an alternative treatment plan. Doctors should listen to their concerns, explain decisions in plain language and provide clear follow-up advice. Responsible prescribing should strengthen trust between doctors and patients, not create conflict.
Why global cooperation matters
AMR crosses national borders and connects human, animal and environmental health. Resistant microorganisms and resistance genes can spread through direct contact, food, water and inadequately managed waste.
The One Health approach recognizes these connections. Reducing unnecessary antimicrobial use in human healthcare, veterinary medicine and agriculture must go hand in hand with vaccination, sanitation, food safety, infection prevention and responsible waste management.
No country can tackle AMR alone. Governments and researchers need to share surveillance data and scientific knowledge, develop faster diagnostic tests, new medicines and vaccines, and help ensure that effective diagnostics and treatments are accessible in lower-resource settings. In May 2026, the World Health Assembly adopted an updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance for 2026–2036, reinforcing the need for coordinated action across sectors.
Protecting tomorrow's medicines starts today
Individuals can help by not taking antibiotics for a common cold without medical advice. Doctors can prescribe carefully and explain their decisions. Hospitals and governments can invest in prevention, surveillance, research and cooperation.
Protecting antibiotics does not mean withholding treatment from patients who need it. It means using these medicines wisely today so they can continue to save lives tomorrow.
The next time a sore throat or runny nose develops, the most useful question may not be, "Which antibiotic should I take?" but rather, "What is causing my symptoms, and what treatment will actually work?"
Group A streptococcus (scanning electron microscope image) 
Editor's note:
Ma Fengjie holds a Doctor of Medicine (M.D.) degree and is a chief physician and chief examining physician at the Institute of Civil Aviation Aircrew Medical Assessment, Civil Aviation Medicine Center of the Civil Aviation Administration of China. He is also a member of the Otorhinolaryngology Group of the Civil Aviation Aircrew Examination and Assessment Expert Committee. His expertise includes the diagnosis and differential diagnosis of ear diseases and hearing-related disorders.

articles.fullText:
Representatives from BRICS countries gather to take part in the International Youth Talk on the Global Civilization Initiative, Fuzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, November 10, 2026. 
In an old riverside building in Fuzhou, southeast China's Fujian Province, young representatives from BRICS countries gathered on Tuesday to discuss how cultural heritage can be preserved, reinterpreted and shared across borders.
The event, titled the International Youth Talk on the Global Civilization Initiative, was held at Zhuzifang Fund Harbor, a historic area where traditional buildings have been preserved and renovated for modern use.
Organized by the China International Youth Exchange Center and hosted by the Fuzhou Youth Federation, the event aimed to promote cross-cultural understanding and encourage young people from different countries to exchange ideas on preserving traditional culture and exploring new forms of cultural expression through digital technologies.
At the event, Zhang Afeng, vice president of the Fujian Youth Federation, highlighted the Global Civilization Initiative (GCI) and its relevance to exchanges among young people.
Proposed by China in March 2023, the GCI calls for respect for the diversity of civilizations, the promotion of common values of humanity, the importance of the inheritance and innovation of civilizations, and stronger international people-to-people exchanges and cooperation.
Zhang said Fujian has maintained close ties with BRICS countries, with cooperation extending beyond trade to areas including healthcare, education, the marine economy and the digital economy. In 2025, trade between Fujian and BRICS countries accounted for nearly one-fifth of the province's total foreign trade, he noted.
He said the Fujian Youth Federation would continue to build platforms for exchanges between Chinese and foreign young people, encouraging them to use technology as a bridge and civilization as a bond to deepen mutual understanding and pursue shared development.
Representatives from BRICS countries pose for a group photo after the International Youth Talk on the Global Civilization Initiative, Fuzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, November 10, 2026. 
Dong Lin, an associate professor at Fujian Polytechnic Normal University, introduced the young participants to Fujian's history and cultural traditions, including folk songs and traditional woodcarving.
The discussion that followed focused on two questions: how young people can pass on traditional culture and bring it into contemporary life, and how digital technologies can create new possibilities for cultural expression.
Participants shared examples of using digital supply chains to bring traditional tea culture to modern consumers, as well as applying digital avatars and artificial intelligence to make traditional lacquerware more accessible and interactive. Others discussed the potential of generative AI and augmented reality to lower barriers to cultural participation and enable people from different backgrounds to take part in cultural creation.
The discussions highlighted how young people can serve not only as inheritors of traditional culture but also as drivers of its renewal. Through technology, creative approaches and cross-cultural collaboration, they can help give cultural heritage new forms of expression and make it more relevant to contemporary audiences.
Several young people from BRICS countries take selfies in the Yantai Hill Historic and Cultural District, Fuzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, November 9, 2026. /China International Youth Exchange Center
The cultural exchange activities also extended beyond the discussion venue.
A day earlier, the young representatives visited Yantai Hill Historic and Cultural District, known for its blend of Chinese and Western architectural styles. They learned about efforts to preserve and renew its historic buildings, pass on architectural heritage and integrate cultural tourism into urban development.
Marwan Elsafty, COO at Grecem, a tech company in Egypt, told CGTN that cultural exchanges help people from different countries find common ground despite differences in their ways of thinking.
“We have some differences, so we need to find the middle ground. How we can find the middle ground? Just by cultural exchange,” he said.
For Anastasia Semenova, CEO of Russian video technology company ViSaver LLC, exchanges are important because people living in their own countries may not fully understand how others view the same events, opportunities or technologies.
“When we all the time live in one country, in our own country, although it's our motherland and beloved, still we don't know how exactly the same things, the same events, the same opportunities, technologies, they are perceived in other countries, how people in other countries think about the same things,” she said.
Siska Pebiana, a researcher at Indonesia's National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), said learning about different cultures can broaden young people's horizons and help them build friendships across borders. She added that being open-minded and understanding different cultural backgrounds makes it easier to connect with people from other countries.
From exploring historic neighborhoods to exchanging ideas on technology and cultural innovation, the exchanges not only reflected the GCI's emphasis on dialogue and mutual learning among civilizations, but highlighted the role young people can play in keeping cultural heritage alive and finding new ways to share it across borders.

What we'll see coming out of APEC are many small, {{5}} changes and recommendations that add up to a great deal in the {{6}}, Stein said. (ECNS) -- Thirty-seven years after its founding, Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) remains committed to advancing trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, and fostering regional economic growth and shared prosperity.
Ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, which will take place in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on Nov. 18–19, foreign business leaders told China News Service that they expect to see stronger policy coordination among APEC economies to promote trade and investment liberalization and facilitation and strengthen cooperation on innovation with the region, while voicing optimism about collaboration with China in clean energy, artificial intelligence and other sectors.
A large delegation of U.S. companies is attending this year's APEC CEO Summit. Sean Stein, president of the U.S.-China Business Council (USCBC), said that many U.S. chief executives hope to see what consensus will be reached across sectors in Shenzhen, which they believe will help them expand the Asia-Pacific market and make cross-border business easier.
What we'll see coming out of APEC are many small, incremental changes and recommendations that add up to a great deal in the aggregate, Stein said.
"Even if it only makes transactions a little tiny bit bigger, think of all the millions of trades and transactions that happen every year across the region," he said.
He described APEC as a vital multilateral platform connecting businesses and governments. Sustained improvements to trade and commercial rules will ease cross-border operations and ultimately benefit consumers throughout the region, he said.
Australia is one of APEC's founding members. Greg Smith, chair of AustCham South China, said Australia "really believes in the community." "Trade within a community is the best way of strengthening understanding and developing commerce and prosperity for all."
Smith hopes APEC members will work together to cut tariffs and further reduce trade restrictions, thus promoting free trade in this area.
Beyond trade facilitation, business leaders are also focused on how Asia-Pacific economies can navigate technological transformation.
Brittany Masalosalo, chief public policy officer at HP Inc, said disruptive technologies are causing governments to rethink how they cooperate, and companies are having to adapt to these challenges as well.
"The Asia Pacific region is one of the most dynamic regions around the world. It's also one of the most diverse regions. Bringing that diversity to bear with the spirit of innovation at this moment is critical. And it's also critical to HP strategy."
For the AI industry, divergent technical standards and governance rules across economies pose hurdles to cross-border collaboration. Alveiro Mateus, co-founder and chief architect of U.S. AI firm OptimOps.ai, said one priority for APEC is to develop standards and governance frameworks that economies can reference and adopt.
Greater alignment on AI safety and reliability, he added, would build trust and unlock more cross-border technology partnerships.
According to China's Ministry of Commerce, China is now the largest trading partner for 13 APEC economies. Expanding economic and trade links between China and its Asia-Pacific counterparts create broader avenues for all parties to share development dividends.
Smith singled out renewable energy and aged care as promising areas for Australia-China collaboration. China's fast-growing electric vehicle and solar panel sectors offer new opportunities for Australian businesses, he said. At the same time, the two sides can "complement each other in responding to population ageing": China brings technological strengths, while Australia boasts a well-established aged-care service system.
Having operated in China for more than four decades, HP continues to find opportunities from China's development.
Masalosalo said China is not only an important part of HP's global manufacturing supply chain but also a major hub for R&D and innovation. Abundant talent from Chinese universities and vibrant local innovators create ample opportunities for partnerships with multinational corporations.
"HP has been proud that we've been able to grow in China, for China, alongside China," she said.
Mateus pointed to complementary strengths in the U.S. and Chinese AI industries, urging stakeholders to explore untapped potential for collaboration.
The U.S. enjoys advantages in R&D and has large models for manufacturing and logistics, while China excels at deploying technology and has strong production capacity, he noted.
Closer collaboration can combine cutting-edge research with large-scale applications in healthcare and manufacturing, delivering more efficient solutions for global markets, he said.

Shen Haixiong, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and president of CMG; Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT); Djauhari Oratmangun, ambassador of the Republic of Indonesia to China; Thaddeus Kambanei, ambassador of the Independent State of Papua New Guinea to China; Carlos Vasquez, ambassador of the Republic of Peru to China; and Ma Mingzhe, chairman of Ping An Group, delivered remarks at the roundtable.

The new roundtable creates a valuable channel for diplomatic envoys and leading Chinese businesses to connect.
China will uphold consistent, stable policies and advance high-quality development and high-standard opening-up.
CCPIT will continue to boost ties between China's business community and Asia-Pacific partners so that the gains from China's modernization drive can unlock fresh opportunities for industrial cooperation across the region.

China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City, departed from Shanghai's Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal on November 9, for its first trial voyage, marking another milestone in the country's efforts to develop its homegrown cruise industry.
The vessel is scheduled to arrive at Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, on November 12. During the voyage, systematic tests and adjustments will be conducted in areas including maritime operations, navigation safety, products and services, ship-shore coordination, and integrated information systems, according to the operator.
China's two domestically built large cruise ships, the Adora Magic City (R) and Adora Flora City (L), docked side by side at Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal in Shanghai, China. /
Under simulated real operating conditions, the trial will also assess key passenger experiences, including cabin services, dining, entertainment, shopping and leisure activities, while testing coordination and response capabilities across different departments. The comprehensive testing marks a crucial step toward the ship's commercial operation. Adora Flora City is scheduled to begin its inaugural season on November 22.
The ship's departure came just one day after a historic scene unfolded at Wusongkou. On November 8, Adora Flora City and Adora Magic City, China's two domestically built large cruise ships, berthed side by side at Shanghai's Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal for the first time. The two vessels sounded their horns to greet each other.
The historic gathering reflects a major step forward for China's shipbuilding industry, from the breakthrough of building its first large cruise ship to developing the capacity for serial production. Large cruise ships are among the most complex engineering projects in the global industrial system, involving extensive coordination across shipbuilding, advanced equipment manufacturing, information technology and supporting industries. The emergence of the two sister ships highlights China's growing capabilities in high-end shipbuilding and industrial integration.
China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City. /
The development of the cruise industry is also closely tied to the transformation of Shanghai's Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal. At the 2026 Wusongkou Forum held at Baoshan District on Sunday, industry representatives highlighted the vision of transforming the port from a cruise home port into a comprehensive hub connecting river and sea transportation, while fostering a broader cruise industry ecosystem.
As a key gateway for China's cruise industry, Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal has maintained its leading position in the country's cruise market for several consecutive years. In the first three quarters of 2026, cruise ship calls and inbound and outbound passenger traffic at the port accounted for 55% and 76% of the respective national totals, according to Baoshan District People's government. The growing presence of international travelers has also become a notable feature of its operations. On March 28, a registered nearly 5,900 passenger visits marked a new record at the terminal for the highest number of inbound foreign passengers in a single day.
The increase in international cruise passengers comes amid China's expanded visa-free entry policies and facilitation of inbound tourism. Cruise travel is also emerging as an important channel for overseas tourists to explore China, with Shanghai serving as a major gateway connecting international travelers to more destinations.

此次全面测试标志着该船向商业运营迈出关键一步。“爱达·花城号”计划于11月22日开启首个航季。该船启航前一天，吴淞口刚刚上演了历史性一幕。11月8日，中国两艘国产大型邮轮“爱达·花城号”和“爱达·魔都号”首次并靠在上海吴淞口国际邮轮港。两艘船鸣笛互致问候。

这一历史性聚首反映出中国造船业向前迈出重要一步：从建造首艘大型邮轮的突破，到形成系列化生产能力。大型邮轮是全球工业体系中最复杂的工程项目之一，涉及造船、先进装备制造、信息技术和配套产业之间的广泛协同。两艘姊妹船的出现凸显了中国在高端造船和产业整合方面不断增强的能力。中国第二艘国产大型邮轮“爱达·花城号”。/ 邮轮产业的发展也与上海吴淞口国际邮轮港的转型密切相关。

在周日于宝山区举行的2026吴淞口论坛上，行业代表强调了将吴淞口从邮轮母港转型为连接江海运输的综合枢纽，同时培育更广泛邮轮产业生态的愿景。作为中国邮轮产业的重要门户，吴淞口国际邮轮港已连续多年保持在中国邮轮市场的领先地位。根据宝山区人民政府的数据，2026年前三季度，该港邮轮靠泊艘次和出入境旅客流量分别占全国总量的55%和76%。国际旅客的日益增多也成为其运营的一个显著特点。3月28日，近5900名注册旅客到访，创下该码头单日入境外国旅客人数的新纪录。

国际邮轮旅客的增长，正值中国扩大免签入境政策并促进入境旅游便利化之际。邮轮旅行也正成为海外游客探索中国的重要渠道，而上海则是连接国际旅客与更多目的地的主要门户。
